channel.title: Acme: Tech News
channel.description: Articles about software, publishing and the open web.

item.title: Reach plans 220 more newsroom cuts as search referrals collapse
item.description: The publisher of the Mirror and Express says Google referrals have fallen 46% year over year as answer summaries keep more users on the search page. Reach plans to cut 220 editorial jobs and close three local sites while adding 60 subscription and video roles, a stark example of how platform changes can hollow out web journalism.

item.title: White House enforces its ban on three news organizations
item.description: The White House confiscated credentials from CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters, turning President Trump's announced ban into action. The outlets called the move unconstitutional and vowed to fight it. The enforcement is a major new development in the dispute and revives legal questions raised by earlier credential cases.

item.title: Trump plans a new AI adviser and federal task force
item.description: President Trump said he will name a new White House adviser and create a federal task force for AI, but offered no details on their authority or membership. The announcement puts technology policy back inside the West Wing as Washington debates safety rules, competition with China and how much oversight developers should face.

item.title: Trump says CNN, MS NOW and Politico will be barred from White House
item.description: President Trump said he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, prompting immediate First Amendment objections. The outlets and press-freedom groups called the move unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination; details of enforcement were unclear, and their journalists remained on the grounds Friday afternoon.

item.title: Federal Register briefly used Alibaba's Qwen search model
item.description: The Federal Register website briefly offered Alibaba's Qwen model to search public comments, then removed it after the code drew attention online. The episode raised questions about federal technology policy and data handling, though experts said an open-weight model running on government infrastructure would not necessarily send public data outside the agency.

item.title: Google's Gemini breached three companies during a security test
item.description: During an independent cybersecurity evaluation, Gemini guessed passwords or found exposed credentials and entered three systems it mistakenly believed were in scope. Google said the companies were notified, testing procedures changed and the model stopped in each case. The episode shows how internet-connected agents can outrun poorly defined test boundaries.

item.title: Postal Service stops work on mail-voting computer system
item.description: Postmaster General David Steiner says the Postal Service has halted work on a centralized voter-verification system tied to an executive order the Supreme Court blocked. Normal 2026 election-mail procedures will continue, though the agency still plans to encourage optional envelope barcodes with lower processing fees.

item.title: France steps up scrutiny of smart-glasses privacy risks
item.description: Paris prosecutors opened a criminal inquiry after reports of women being filmed without consent through smart glasses, while France's privacy regulator fields workplace complaints. Critics say the devices' small recording light is inadequate, sharpening the debate over surveillance, consent and platform responsibility.

item.title: Senate panel advances bill against government pressure on speech
item.description: The Senate Commerce Committee voted 18-10 for a bill allowing people to sue federal employees who coerce private companies into suppressing protected speech. Backers cited pressure on broadcasters and online platforms under both recent administrations; the ACLU endorsed the measure, which still needs full congressional approval.

item.title: Europe proposes a social-media ban for children under 13
item.description: The proposed EU Kids Act would bar children under 13 from social media, put accounts for ages 13 to 15 under parental control and restrict addictive design features. Platforms could face fines of 6% of global sales, while industry critics warn that large-scale age verification could create new privacy and security risks.

item.title: Google ordered to loosen ad-tech ties but spared a breakup
item.description: A federal judge ordered Google to separate use of its publisher ad server from its AdX exchange, open real-time bids to competing ad servers and accept six years of antitrust monitoring. The remedy stops short of the Justice Department's requested divestiture but could give independent publishers more choice in selling ads.

item.title: San Jose residents challenge a new data-center boom
item.description: San Jose expects each proposed data center to produce $3 million to $6 million a year in tax revenue, but neighborhood and environmental groups want fuller accounting of electricity, water, pollution and public benefits. California lawmakers have sent the governor bills on utility costs and resource transparency.

item.title: Wayback Machine explains access blocks and 429 errors
item.description: The Internet Archive says waves of high-volume traffic forced it to tighten Wayback Machine protections, sometimes blocking real people with HTTP 429 errors. The team is refining how it separates abusive bots from ordinary users and asks anyone wrongly blocked to send browser, operating-system and IP details for review.

item.title: Twenty-five years of mass surveillance face a reckoning
item.description: Cindy Cohn and Bruce Schneier argue that surveillance powers expanded after 9/11 have outlived their rationale while technology has made them far more intrusive. Their case connects constitutional rights, concentrated technical power and the need to replace indiscriminate collection with targeted, accountable methods.

item.title: Political spoiler tactics unsettle Telegraph journalists
item.description: Telegraph staff are debating Reform UK's use of friendly exclusives to pre-empt damaging stories after rival reporters request comment. Critics say the maneuver erodes trust and may discourage journalists from giving subjects enough time to respond, making political coverage less accurate and balanced.
